text: Some time later, a small inheritance allowed May Bartram to settle in a little house in London, and there Marcher began to visit her regularly, as a man returns to a familiar shelter. <break time="0.8s" /> They often went to the opera together, and in the course of the years their talk returned again and again, sometimes lightly and sometimes gravely, to the thing that lay in wait for him. <break time="0.8s" /> Marcher told himself that a man in his position could not decently marry, for, as he put it, a man of feeling does not ask a lady to accompany him on a tiger hunt. <break time="0.8s" /> The Beast, he believed, was crouching somewhere in the jungle of his days, ready to spring, and it seemed only fair that he alone should face whatever danger its leap might bring. <break time="0.8s" /> Their friends and acquaintances, seeing them so often together, naturally supposed that there was some romance between them, and May allowed this appearance to serve as a screen for the secret that they actually shared. <break time="0.8s" /> I have helped you to pass for a man like another, she once said, and Marcher, grateful for her kindness, never asked himself what this long service might be costing her. <break time="0.8s" /> Year after year he gave her small presents on her birthday, and he congratulated himself on being unselfish, never suspecting that his whole attention, all the while, was fixed upon himself.
